title: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
description: "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.He then held up a photo
body: "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York.He then held up a photo of the country's late Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike on his residence when the US and Israel launched a joint attack in late February.He also presented pictures of some of the more than 175 civilians, two thirds of them children, who Iranian authorities say were killed in missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd that day. The US has denied striking Lamerd and said it is still investigating what happened in Minab."Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said.Also on Wednesday, an attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz killed an Indian sailor, the Agence France-Presse news agency reported, citing Omani and Indian authorities. The attack was condemned by India's foreign ministry, which called for unimpeded passage through the Strait to be restored. In February, Iran retaliated for the massive US-Israeli air campaign by launching deadly missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, by attacking commercial vessels in the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The US responded by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports and ships in April.In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran wants to retain some measure of control over the strait and collect fees from vessels that use it, which the US has rejected.In his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a "big decision" - either negotiate a deal that would allow Iranians to rebuild their country, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly".Pezeshkian said the threat was "a sign of a bullying mentality"."[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend the knee," he said.But he added: "We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force."Pezeshkian made clear that the US blockade would have to end as part of any deal."It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway," he said.He also reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to have a civilian nuclear programme and that it would not seek to develop nuclear weapons."We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations on peaceful nuclear technology."Trump argued in his speech that the war had prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb and demanded that its leaders "relinquish their nuclear ambitions".On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work.But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

schema.headline: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'

title: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
description: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's ho
body: The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis.The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it.Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650.It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350.Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti.Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building.In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money".The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead."Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez.A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes. In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year.The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed".However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

schema.headline: Maricarmen: Eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage

title: South Africa mass shooting: Gunmen kill 11 at house in Durban
description: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.Gunmen stormed a house in the K
body: At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban.Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said.Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched".While the motive of the shooting has not yet been confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings". "Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died.A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car.The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects, who were said to be carrying pistols and rifles.South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day.In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country.Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg.Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities.In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police.Although South Africa has long had a high murder rate, mass shootings are a more recent problem and elicit increased feelings of unsafety, fear and shock. The phenomenon has led to calls for the government and law enforcement authorities to do more to dismantle organised crime networks and, in some cases, "murder for hire" syndicates – believed to be among the leading instigators of the attacks. Much has also been said about improving the economic conditions that make crime an attractive enterprise for some. There are no easy answers for how to solve South Africa's crime problem but security experts believe that the high proliferation of illegal guns, insufficient visible policing in high crime spots, the slow pace of justice and allegations that senior politicians and police officers have links to criminal gangs all add to the pervasive sentiment that local authorities are losing the fight against crime.

schema.headline: South Africa mass shooting: Gunmen kill 11 at house in Durban

title: Oleshky: Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
description: Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedByOlga Malche
body: Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedByOlga Malchevska"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakova Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.Image source, Maxar Technologies Handout/EPA-EFE/REX/ShutterstockImage caption, Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023.Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive."There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May."I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutionsWhich weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearWarning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below.Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east.Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information."I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety."They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana. Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky.Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish."This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine."If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says.Figure caption, Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone

schema.headline: Oleshky: Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water

title: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
description: Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces rema
body: Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert.Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo.It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately.Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this.Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar.Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added.A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato.Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank."In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said."The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response".Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

schema.headline: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace

title: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
description: For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent histor
body: For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table."A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department."When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said."A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated."Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials. Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings."People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it."You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children."There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."The ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has once again sparked political debate in the US.After the state health department announced the first two deaths - both in infants - Kennedy, the top health official, took to social media to dispute at least one of the deaths. The BBC has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro took aim at Kennedy, saying he told the top US health official that he was spreading misinformation that was worsening the outbreak.Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican, has said one of the two infants died of a ruptured spleen rather than measles itself. Measles can cause the spleen to enlarge, making it more likely to rupture. Several doctors have said the measles infection made the child vulnerable."I think the measles very much contributed to that child's demise," said William Moss, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.Public health experts said a number of actions taken by Kennedy and the Trump administration have sowed doubts about vaccine safety and worsened outbreaks.Last month, Trump passed an executive order recommending the MMR shot be split into three separate shots, a move doctors say is costly and unnecessary for a vaccine that is already safe."What he's doing is casting doubt," said Dr Moss. "He basically said the vaccine could be dangerous in its current combined form."The tensions are not helpful for experts working to combat misinformation in a so-far unrelenting outbreak, they said. They worry for the start of the school year, which will provide even more opportunities for the highly contagious virus to spread."I think we're in this for six to 12 months. It does feel like it's spreading and accelerating," Weiser said. "We're in community transmission now. We can't stop it easily."

schema.headline: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles

title: Why the Dutch dictionary has a new word for labia
description: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labiaImage source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating
body: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labiaImage source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new wordBySmitha MundasadHealth reporter Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental."Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame"."It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.'Sex positivity'Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.Image source, Shari KleinImage caption, Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls"Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaamhaar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaambeen" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaamluis" for pubic lice.However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change Schamlippen to "Vulvalippen".Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame."Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.'Virginity membrane'Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once."With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".Image source, Luciano ÖlzImage caption, Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."'Judgmental words'Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first."Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue."Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected."Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress."I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."

schema.headline: Why the Dutch dictionary has a new word for labia

title: Dopamine sites: India and the world are discovering the thrill of shopping without buying
description: Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen'ByIndia correspondentYou are hungry. Or you are not. It do
body: Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen'ByIndia correspondentYou are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen."Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June. It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience. Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, The site offers 22 fake kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel. What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".Image source, Purvansh ParmarImage caption, Purvansh Parmar says he spent a lot of money on a work trip on food and treats he did not necessarily needWhat begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared."Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Swiggy, a popular food delivery site in India, alone handled roughly 2.5m consumer orders a day in FY2025 Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience"."Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction."To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."Image caption, TripNeverLeaves lets users plan a holiday before sending them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway.What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'". But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve. "While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A festive sale of of e-commerce site in India featuring Bollywood star Amitabh BachchanBut there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace. Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate"."The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset."I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.Image caption, TripNeverLeaves lists 260 places 'you won't go'The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain"."In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

schema.headline: Dopamine sites: India and the world are discovering the thrill of shopping without buying

title: Trump and Xi meet as AI rivalry reshapes global power dynamics
description: AI superpower ambitions take centre stage as Trump and Xi meetImage source, ReutersImage caption, The US and China are locked in a race to develop AIB
body: AI superpower ambitions take centre stage as Trump and Xi meetImage source, ReutersImage caption, The US and China are locked in a race to develop AIByJoe TidyCyber correspondent and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporter"Whoever wins AI, WINS!"US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view."China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax".China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.Is the US in the lead?There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external.Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI developmentThe stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success.Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.China's advantageDespite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said."AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."Image source, Future Publishing via Getty ImagesImage caption, Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service."Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".Safety concerns?China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president."We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.Image source, VCG via Getty ImagesImage caption, China is the world's biggest manufacturer of robotsBeijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control"."China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.Will they cooperate?Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said."Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.What we don't want, she added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.

schema.headline: Trump and Xi meet as AI rivalry reshapes global power dynamics

title: Morocco election: How Ceuta, football and Israel have shaped the campaign
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Moroccan voters will find candidates from 27 parties on the ballotByBasma El AttiDisillusioned young
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Moroccan voters will find candidates from 27 parties on the ballotByBasma El AttiDisillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality."I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.Image source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, Some 60,000 people swam from Morocco to the Spanish territory of Ceuta in late JulyHamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda."As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history."We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031."As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."Image source, Fifa via Getty ImagesImage caption, Morocco's FA president Fouzi Lekjaa is beloved by fans for helping put the Atlas Lions on the world football stageFouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise."The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Huge pro-Palestinian protests often take place in RabatAlso seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on  a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations."We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh."If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".Siham AzeroualI think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24."I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot."Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach."I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.You may also be interested in:

schema.headline: Morocco election: How Ceuta, football and Israel have shaped the campaign

title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault
description: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a crimin
body: Disgraced Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years in prison, after a jury found him guilty last year of committing a criminal sexual act against a former assistant.In a victim-impact statement in court, Miriam Haley said the assault had had a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away".Appearing in court in a wheelchair, Weinstein denied the allegations but apologised to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions". Weinstein has already spent several years jailed in New York, where he has faced three trials over rape and abuse allegations. He was convicted in a separate sex-crime case in Los Angeles. This is the second time he has been given a prison sentence in the Miriam Haley case. Weinstein was first convicted and sentenced in 2020, but New York's highest court overturned the conviction in 2024, along with another involving actress Jessica Mann. The court ruled that Weinstein did not get a fair trial.He was retried and convicted again last year on a single charge of a criminal sexual act against Haley.Weinstein, 74, is currently being held in a prison ward at New York's Bellevue Hospital for a series of ailments reported during his incarceration.Once the high-flying producer behind Miramax, the studio that produced hits like Shakespeare in Love, Weinstein fell from grace in 2017 after the New York Times and the New Yorker revealed multiple women's allegations of sexual assault stretching back decades. The accusations against him sparked the #MeToo movement, but New York prosecutors have had to navigate a twisting path in securing convictions and sentences.In the 2020 trial, Haley testified that Weinstein had assaulted her in a bedroom in his Manhattan apartment in 2006. Haley was a production assistant on the Project Runway television series at the time. On charges related to Mann, juries could not reach a verdict, and he was found not guilty in another charge involving model Kaja Sokola. After testifying in the retrial last year, Haley told the BBC she felt compelled to take the stand. "I just thought, I have to stand up for myself. I have to stand up for the truth," she said.Weinstein is still awaiting sentencing in the California, where he was convicted in 2022 of raping and sexually assaulting an actress in a hotel room in 2013. An appeals court ordered he be re-sentenced in the case after the New York convictions were overturned.Weinstein has consistently denied the allegations against him, and said he believes he will be proven innocent.On Wednesday, Judge Curtis Farber criticised the former Hollywood mogul as he announced the 15-year sentence."You took what you wanted by force and you have never accepted responsibility," Farber said.

schema.headline: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in prison for sexual assault

title: Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first
description: A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data in what experts say is the first known case of its kind
body: A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data in what experts say is the first known case of its kind in the world.The agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in New York on Wednesday, local time.He had a "very frank discussion" with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for taking "too long" to disclose the breach and said there would be "legal consequences".OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.Five days later, that government agency, Services Australia, escalated the email to Australia's cybersecurity centre before a government minister was notified and the prime minister alerted.Albanese said he spoke to Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" as well as his "disappointment" that the company had taken months to reveal the breach and "the nature of the way" it did so.The Australian leader said Altman had acknowledged there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.A "forensic investigation" led by the country's cybersecurity agency would aim to find out if other government systems were affected, Albanese said.The probe would also assess if the matter needed to be dealt with by police, he said, noting there "will obviously be legal consequences".Detailing the breach, Albanese said it had involved "public and non-public files" on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, home to "non-sensitive" data and statistics.Three other government systems "may" also have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and two state-based agencies - the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health."No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing," Albanese said."Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable," he said.OpenAI, in a statement, said it had "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation". "In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," the statement said.Albanese declined to answer whether he raised the matter with US President Donald Trump during their face-to-face meeting on Tuesday night in New York, where world leaders have gathered for the UN General Assembly.Australia was one of 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for the development of AI. Cybersecurity experts told the BBC the incident is a wake up call for regulators, given that AI agents are becoming more widely available for individual and commercial use.Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of NSW Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC that though this is the first known incident where AI agents have chosen to breach a government body of their own volition, there'll be more to come."I expect that these kinds of attacks will keep occurring," he said, adding that they would likely "grow in severity and in frequency"."I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firm named Hugging Face.And a string of other rogue AI incidents have also been made public this year, including a case where a digital assistant - without instruction - booted someone off a pilates class waiting list in a bid to get an Australian man in.Several AI firm leaders themselves - including Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk - have said the speed at which AI is developing is dangerous to humanity and needs to be reined in.But the US and China, who are vying for AI supremacy, are roadblocks. Both are hostile to greater regulation, wanting the economic and technological spoils of AI, and have downplayed safety concerns.

schema.headline: Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first

title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction
description: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN Gene
body: US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280m handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade.Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason"."The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year."All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that". Michael Eisenberg, an Israeli-American Board of Peace member, told the BBC's Newshour programme what the next steps were likely to be."Because it's a war zone, you need to remove unexploded ordnance. And then there are still hundreds of kilometres of tunnels underneath Gaza which need to be destroyed as well."Once that's all done, Gazans can get to rebuilding again: whether it's housing, or better sanitation, or other things," Eisenberg said.In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of Hamas.In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year. Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza. But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.

schema.headline: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction

title: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
description: Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a
body: Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict.Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray.The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal.It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Ethiopian President Taye Astike Selassie said his country had shown "immense restraint" in its actions despite "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements", without specifying who those elements were.He added: "Our message to forces of destruction and mayhem is loud and clear. We urge them to respect the sacred right of the people of the Horn of Africa to live in peace and prosperity."On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray,  announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.Getachew said in a statement shared on social media: "It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara." The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government.Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.The chairperson of the Africa Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has called for an "immediate de-escalation" and for both sides to resume talks.The US ambassador to Ethiopia condemned the TPLF for making "the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive", describing it as an "unwinnable fight".On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30."This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes.On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted.Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022.In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.

schema.headline: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war

title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation
description: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's lega
body: Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests.The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week.The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him.In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims.In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people."Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said."A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's  security detail for the last 20 years of her life.Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties.In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained".They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much."The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell.The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand.In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents.Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me."The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees.In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police."All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint.In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer."But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents.She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states.The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment.Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August. Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video.Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years.Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager.In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career.In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death."She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement."Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come."The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton's manager accuses nephew who announced her death of threats and intimidation
